title: recite
text:
Display lines are grouped into render pieces. A piece closes after a word holding a daṇḍa, so the two pādas of a hemistich printed as two lines render as one piece, as Vāgdhenu expects. Prose closes too at max_syll akṣaras; verse closes before a line that would pass max_verse. Each piece keeps (line, word) for every word, so timings can go back to the lines; a word that cleans to nothing (a daṇḍa, a verse number) stays, untimed.

title: recite
text:
Reciting sections
A section is recited in parts, each in one voice. By default the section is split into verses, each closing on a line with a double daṇḍa, and ganapati scans each: it applies the śloka’s rules (Vāgdhenu’s own detector passed a 32-syllable prose sentence as anuṣṭubh) and knows the āryā family. A metre in Vāgdhenu’s bank is chanted against its reference, another vṛtta against the fallback (vasantatilakā), and an āryā-family metre or none is read. A caller can pass its own parts, dict(lines=[…], meter=…), and kind forces one voice for the whole section. Each part takes the best of tries seeds by Su-śrotā’s error rate.

A stand-in chanter and ear check the bookkeeping without the models: a verse that scans is chanted, the prose after it is read, and the second part’s timings start after the first part and the gap.

from vachaka.core import Recitation
from vachaka.check import Ear
class FakeCh:
    gap, prose_gap = 0.5, 0.3
    def meter(self, lines): return 'anushtubh' if len(lines) == 2 else ''
    def bank_ref(self, name): return {'anuṣṭubh': 'anuṣṭubh', 'mālinī': 'mālinī'}.get(name)
    def render(self, ps, ref, seed, gap): return Recitation(np.zeros(len(ps)*24000, np.float32), [(i*1000, i*1000+900) for i in range(len(ps))], ps)
class FakeEar:
    def hear(self, audio, sr): return ''
    heard = Ear.heard   # best_of hears a render a piece at a time
    def words(self, rec, ws): return [[[w, s, e] for w in p] for (s,e),p in zip(rec.spans, ws)]
r, info = recite_section(FakeCh(), FakeEar(), ['धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।', 'मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय ॥ १ ॥', 'इति प्रश्नः ॥'])
test_eq([p['kind'] for p in info['parts']], ['chant', 'read'])
test_eq(info['kind'], 'mixed')
test_eq(info['lines'][2]['s'], 2000 + 800)           # two 1 s pieces, then the gap
_, info = recite_section(FakeCh(), FakeEar(), ['क ख ग', 'घ ङ च ॥', 'छ ज झ ।'])
test_eq([p['kind'] for p in info['parts']], ['chant', 'read'])  # the line after the verse is its own part, and scans as nothing
ps = [dict(lines=[0, 1], meter='mālinī'), dict(lines=[2], meter='āryā'), dict(lines=[3], meter='śikhariṇī'), dict(lines=[4], meter=None)]
_, info = recite_section(FakeCh(), FakeEar(), ['क ।', 'ख ॥', 'ग ॥', 'घ ॥', 'ङ ।'], parts=ps)
test_eq([(p['kind'], p['ref']) for p in info['parts']], [('chant', 'mālinī'), ('read', 'anuṣṭubh'), ('chant', 'vasantatilaka'), ('read', 'anuṣṭubh')])

title: check
text: Su-śrotā is IndicConformer fine-tuned on śāstric Sanskrit. Its CTC head covers all 22 IndicConformer languages; Sanskrit is the 256 columns from 4096, with the blank at 5632. The checkpoint’s config names AI4Bharat’s NeMo fork (multilingual tokenizer, multisoftmax decoder), so Ear rewrites it for upstream NeMo: the tokenizer becomes agg, the fork-only keys go, and the weights load non-strict. Only the encoder and the CTC head are used. Install with pip install vachaka[check].

title: check
text:
Best of a few seeds
A render whose transcript is far from its text is retried with the next seed; the closest is kept. Recitation.cer records how far it was. The transcript is heard a piece at a time: heard whole, a long run of near-identical lines (a tarpaṇa, the eight quarters of a digvandana) makes the recogniser lose its place, and a good render scored 0.47-0.76.

Ear.heard
def heard(
    rec
):
What Su-śrotā hears of rec, each piece of spans on its own, joined.



class _E(Ear):
    def __init__(self): self.got = []
    def hear(self, audio, sr): self.got.append(len(audio)); return 'क'
e, r = _E(), AttrDict(audio=np.zeros(16000*3, np.float32), sr=16000, spans=[(0, 1000), (1500, 3000)])
test_eq(e.heard(r), 'क क'); test_eq(e.got, [16000, 24000])
test_eq(_E().heard(AttrDict(audio=np.zeros(800, np.float32), sr=16000)), 'क')

title: check
text:
Word timings
Each piece’s words are force-aligned within that piece’s span, so one bad line cannot drag the rest. Words are given as displayed; each is tokenised from its cleaned form, and a word with no Sanskrit tokens (a lone daṇḍa) gets an empty span at its neighbour’s end.


source

Ear.words
def words(
    rec, words
):
For each piece of rec and its list of displayed words, [word, start_ms, end_ms] per word.


These need the Su-śrotā checkpoint (520 MB) and the Vāgdhenu weights, so they do not run in the tests.

from vachaka.core import Chanter
ch, ear = Chanter(), Ear()
lines = ['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्']
r = best_of(partial(ch.chant, lines), ear, ' '.join(lines))
r.cer, ear.words(r, [l.split() for l in lines])

title: vachaka
text:
vachaka turns Devanagari into recited audio and tells you where every line and word falls in it. It is a thin layer over two models by Prathosh A. P.: Vāgdhenu, a metre-aware chant TTS (an IndicF5 fine-tune with a BigVGAN-v2 vocoder), and Su-śrotā, a Sanskrit ASR (IndicConformer fine-tuned on śāstric Sanskrit). Vāgdhenu does the speaking. Su-śrotā listens back: it scores each render against its text, so a bad seed can be thrown away, and it force-aligns the words.
It was written for VedicReader, which has thousands of Sanskrit verses and sūtras with no recording. The input there is a title’s display lines, and the output has to be one audio file plus a [start, end] for every line and word, so the reader can follow along. That is what vachaka.recite does.

Numbers
Measured on an Apple M3 Max (36 GB), with the DiT on MPS and the vocoder on the CPU.







loading Vāgdhenu
10 to 17 s

about 5.5 s per second of audio (a 9.5 s anuṣṭubh verse in 50 to 57 s)


share of render time in the DiT
77% (the rest is BigVGAN on the CPU)


loading Su-śrotā
9 s


transcribing a 10 s clip on the CPU
0.4 s


alignment resolution
40 ms (Su-śrotā’s frame)



At that speed an hour of recitation takes five to six hours on a laptop. A CUDA GPU is much faster; Vāgdhenu’s author renders on one.
The pilot rendered 27 sections (293 s of audio) from a stotra, three jyotiṣa books, the Jaimini Sūtras and the Nyāyasūtra, taking the best of up to three seeds per section:

Two cautions. Su-śrotā comes from the same lab and its training data includes a TTS-speaker slice, so it may hear Vāgdhenu more kindly than a person would; a low CER says the words are there, not that the chant is beautiful. And a section whose metre is not detected (āryā, a verse split over three lines) is read as prose, which sounds flatter than a chant. Listen before you ship.

title: vachaka
text:
Install
pip install vachaka            # rendering
pip install 'vachaka[check]'   # Su-śrotā: transcripts, error rate, word timings
Python 3.10 to 3.12. The first Chanter() downloads about 1.5 GB of weights from the Hugging Face Hub and fetches the sources of Vāgdhenu, BigVGAN and IndicF5 at pinned commits into ~/.cache/vachaka (set VACHAKA_CACHE to move it); none of the three is on PyPI, and the f5-tts that is differs from IndicF5. Su-śrotā is 520 MB more. Writing mp3 needs ffmpeg.

title: vachaka
text:
Use
Chant a verse given as its lines, and read prose:
from vachaka.core import Chanter
ch = Chanter()                        # cuda, then mps, then cpu
r = ch.chant(['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्'])
r.spans                               # [(0, 4230), (4980, 9550)]: one span per line, in ms
r.save('krishna.mp3')
ch.read('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा । चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ।', ref='anuṣṭubh').save('mimamsa.mp3')
Check a render and time its words:
from vachaka.check import Ear, best_of
ear = Ear()
lines = ['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्']
r = best_of(lambda seed: ch.chant(lines, seed=seed), ear, ' '.join(lines))
r.cer                                 # 0.0
ear.hear(r.audio, r.sr)               # 'वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनं देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुं'
ear.words(r, [l.split() for l in lines])
# [[['वसुदेवसुतं', 120, 1279], ['देवं', 1279, 1878], ['कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 1878, 3756]],
#  [['देवकीपरमानन्दं', 5100, 7018], ['कृष्णं', 7018, 7697], ['वन्दे', 7697, 8217], ['जगद्गुरुम्', 8217, 9056]]]
Recite whole sections from their display lines, with daṇḍas, verse numbers and accents left in; each line comes back with its span and words:
from vachaka.recite import recite
rec, info = recite(ch, ear, [dict(lines=['नित्यानन्दकरी वराभयकरी सौन्दर्यरत्नाकरी', 'निर्धूताखिलघोरपावनकरी प्रत्यक्षमाहेश्वरी ।',
                                         'प्रालेयाचलवंशपावनकरी काशीपुराधीश्वरी', 'भिक्षां देहि कृपावलम्बनकरी मातान्नपूर्णेश्वरी ॥ १ ॥'])])
info[0]['kind'], info[0]['ref'], info[0]['lines'][0]   # 'chant', 'shardulavikridita', {'s': ..., 'e': ..., 'w': [...]}
For batches there is a resumable CLI over jsonl: vachaka-recite jobs.jsonl results.jsonl, where a job is dict(id, out, sections).

title: vachaka
text:
How it works
recite groups display lines into pieces, closing a piece after a daṇḍa, so the two pādas of a hemistich printed on two lines render together, as Vāgdhenu expects. Each verse (closing on a double daṇḍa) is scanned by ganapati: one in a metre from Vāgdhenu’s bank is chanted against that metre’s reference clip, another vṛtta against vasantatilakā, and an āryā or anything that does not scan is read in chunks of at most 24 akṣaras. So a commentary that quotes a verse chants the verse and reads the rest. Vāgdhenu renders each piece separately and joins them with short silences; vachaka records where each piece landed. Su-śrotā then transcribes the whole render, and if the error rate is above 8% the section is rendered again with another seed, keeping the best of three. Finally the words of each piece are force-aligned (torchaudio’s CTC aligner on Su-śrotā’s posteriors) inside that piece’s span, so one bad line can’t pull the rest out of place.
Two things had to be patched to run this on a Mac. BigVGAN’s transposed convolution has more than 65,536 output channels, which MPS rejects, so the vocoder runs on the CPU. And Su-śrotā’s checkpoint names AI4Bharat’s NeMo fork; vachaka rewrites its config for upstream NeMo (the tokenizer type becomes agg, the fork’s multisoftmax keys go) and uses only the encoder and the CTC head, the Sanskrit columns 4096 to 4351.

title: vachaka
text:
Limits
No Vedic svaras: Vāgdhenu is laukika chant, and accents are stripped before rendering. One voice, the model author’s. The reference clip sets pace and melody but not timbre. Metres outside Vāgdhenu’s bank fall back to vasantatilakā when detected as some other vṛtta, and to prose when not detected at all. Prose sounds like careful reading, not chant.

text:

vachaka is Apache-2.0. Vāgdhenu (code Apache-2.0; weights redistributed under IndicF5’s MIT and NVIDIA BigVGAN’s licence) and Su-śrotā (fine-tuned from AI4Bharat’s IndicConformer, MIT) are by Prathosh A. P.; please cite Vāgdhenu if you use its audio. The model card asks that the voice not be used to impersonate anyone. Say that the audio is synthetic wherever you publish it.

title: core
text:
Vāgdhenu (code, weights, Apache-2.0) is an IndicF5 fine-tune with a BigVGAN-v2 vocoder, trained on one speaker’s chant. Its source, BigVGAN’s and IndicF5’s (f5_tts, which differs from the f5-tts on PyPI) are not pip packages, so all three are fetched at pinned commits into the cache on first use and put on sys.path. title: core
text:
Text
The model reads plain Devanagari. Vedic accents, digits, and verse numbers between daṇḍas are dropped. Vāgdhenu has no svaras and is for laukika chant.

    s

Plain Devanagari for the model: no accents, digits or numbered daṇḍas.



test_eq(clean('अग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं ॥ १ ॥'), 'अग्निमीळे पुरोहितं ॥')
test_eq(clean('धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे ।'), 'धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे ।')

    s

Akṣaras in Devanagari s: independent vowels and consonants not killed by a virāma.



test_eq(n_syll('कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते'), 8)

chunk_prose
def chunk_prose(
    text, max_syll:int=24
):
Split prose at daṇḍas, then at word breaks, into pieces of at most max_syll akṣaras.



p = chunk_prose('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा । चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः । तस्य निमित्तपरीष्टिः ॥')
test_eq(p, ['अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा', 'चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः', 'तस्य निमित्तपरीष्टिः'])
assert all(n_syll(c) <= 24 for c in chunk_prose('क '*80))

text:
Sound
Named treatments for someone who is not a sound engineer, chosen by ear. Each ends in loudness normalisation (-16 LUFS), so every title plays at the same volume, and none moves a sound in time: an echo adds decay after a syllable, never delay before it, so the line and word timings hold. warm is the default: a little warmth below 250 Hz, a soft de-esser and the short echo of a small room. phone lifts the words for small speakers.

title: core
text:
Chanter
Loads the DiT, the vocoder and the reference bank once. pace stretches every syllable (1.15 by default: unhurried, for chanting along). On Apple silicon the DiT runs on MPS and BigVGAN on the CPU, since MPS lacks a transposed convolution with more than 65,536 output channels. chant renders verse against the bank’s reference for the metre ganapati scans it as; read renders prose against the gadya reference by default. The reference sets pace and melody; the timbre is the fine-tuned voice.


source

Chanter
def Chanter(
    voice:str='steer', device:NoneType=None, nfe:int=64, speed:float=0.9, gap:float=0.55, prose_gap:float=0.3,
    tail:float=0.18, fade:float=0.12, pad:float=0.5, pace:float=1.15
):
Sanskrit verse and prose to audio with line spans.


Rendering needs the weights (about 1.5 GB on first use) and takes several times real time on Apple silicon, so these cells do not run in the tests.

ch = Chanter()
r = ch.chant(['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्'])
r.spans, r.save('/tmp/krishna.mp3')
